overview: These records trace two stages of Montenegro’s earlier political history: the eighteenth-century world of Cetinje’s bishops and the later internationally recognised state. The imported outlines appear too broad for their earlier dates, especially before the Balkan Wars; they should not be treated as precise historical borders. The nineteenth-century household objects, school and book described below belong to that later development, not automatically to the 1715 snapshot.

periods.title: Bishops and regional leaders
periods.summary: The Petrović bishops worked alongside assemblies and other powerful leaders.

periods.title: A developing principality
periods.summary: An 1852 assembly separated secular and church authority before later international recognition.

periods.title: Recognised independence
periods.summary: European powers recognised the state; war and its aftermath later ended separate rule.

sections.title: Early power had to be negotiated

items.text: Danilo Petrović was chosen as metropolitan of Cetinje in 1697. Religious and political leadership overlapped, while local leaders remained powerful. Decisions depended on assemblies, alliances and negotiation as well as the bishop’s personal authority.

In 1713, a court of sixteen leading men was created to settle serious disputes between clans and communities. It lacked reliable means to enforce every judgment. Creating a court and making its decisions effective were separate tasks.

Montenegro also had governors, or guvernadurs, alongside the bishops. The museum’s statehood display traces this office from 1717 to its abolition in 1830. Competing institutions help explain why the earlier country cannot be pictured as a modern administration run by one ruler.

A billiard table brought from Austria in 1840 stands in Njegoš’s former residence. The building became known as Biljarda. Government, literature and an indoor game met in the same setting; even a prince-bishop could enjoy trying to make a difficult shot.

Cetinje’s secular school opened in 1834, initially serving boys from wealthier families. The museum exhibits photographs of the monastery setting and the later school at Dobrsko Selo. Schooling expanded through particular institutions, with access much narrower than universal education.

The Cetinje printing house produced teaching books, official proclamations and the journal Grlica in 1835. Preserved examples show how print supported both learning and government. The press connected the work of setting individual letters with public communication across the country.

sections.title: Household objects from the later period

items.text: The nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnographic collection includes elliptical wooden barrels called burilos for carrying and storing water. Wooden strips were held together with metal hoops. Before a tap could be assumed, a household needed suitable containers and somebody to bring the water home.

A household display brings together a cradle, children’s toys, a wooden dough tray and iron equipment for a hearth. A cooking pot could hang from chains above the fire. These objects place childcare and food preparation in the same busy domestic space.

For a family patron saint’s celebration, special bread could be marked with a carved wooden seal. One displayed type bears abbreviated Greek Christian lettering. The loaf joined cooking with religious observance, while the seal allowed the same design to be pressed into fresh dough.

Danilo I hospital opened at Cetinje in 1873. Petar Miljanić later directed it from 1884 to 1897 and practised both surgery and eye medicine. The hospital’s documented staff and building show the growth of organised medical services in the later principality.

The title “Горскій віенацЪ” means “The Mountain Wreath”. These are the historical Cyrillic forms transcribed in the Matica Srpska Library’s catalogue of Njegoš’s 1847 edition. The book is catalogued as Serbian; its older spelling differs from the modern form of the title.

That edition was printed by the Mechitarist press in Vienna, with a portrait and 116 numbered pages. A Montenegrin ruler’s work therefore depended on printing beyond his own state. The surviving book connects local literary creation with an international network of production.

ending.text: In 1918 an assembly deposed King Nikola and voted to merge Montenegro with Serbia, leading into the new Yugoslav kingdom. The decision was contested, and diplomatic recognition lingered: the United States withdrew recognition in 1920. Neither imported endpoint marks the disappearance of Montenegrin communities.
